opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it helps to sort the approaches into a few buckets, because they're often lumped together and they have pretty different strengths and failure modes.

The first bucket is inference-time techniques: chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, sampling many outputs and voting, tree search over candidate reasoning paths. These clearly help on certain benchmarks, especially math and coding where you can check the answer. But I'd be cautious about reading too much into the gains. A lot of the improvement comes from spending more compute and trying more times, which is a perfectly legitimate engineering trade-off, but it's different from the model "understanding" the problem better. And the cost matters. If you need a hundred samples to get a reliable answer, that changes the economics of a deployment quite a bit.

The second bucket is training-time approaches, especially reinforcement learning on reasoning traces with verifiable rewards. That's where much of the recent progress has come from, and I think it's real. The catch is that it works best in domains with a cheap, reliable verifier, like math competitions, unit tests, or formal proofs. Most of what people actually want from AI in the real world, like legal judgment, medical decisions, or business strategy, doesn't come with a ground-truth checker. So there's an open question about how far this generalizes outside the domains where it's easy to measure.

The third bucket is tool use and scaffolding: letting the model call a code interpreter, a search engine, or a symbolic solver. Pragmatically, I find this one the most promising, because it acknowledges that the language model doesn't have to do everything itself. A lot of reasoning failures turn out to be things like arithmetic errors or failures to retrieve a fact, and those are better handled by tools.

Cutting across all of this is my bigger concern, which is evaluation. Sayash Kapoor and I have written a lot about how benchmark performance can mislead. There's contamination, where test problems leak into training data. There's overfitting to the benchmark format. And there's a construct validity problem: a high score on a reasoning benchmark doesn't necessarily mean the model will reason reliably in a messy real-world setting where the problem isn't neatly specified. We've seen many cases where a model aces the leaderboard and then stumbles on trivially perturbed versions of the same questions.

So my overall assessment is that there's genuine progress, especially in verifiable domains, but we should be humble about what it implies. I'd like the field to put as much effort into rigorous, deployment-relevant evaluation, including cost, reliability, and how often a human has to step in, as it puts into pushing the frontier on benchmark numbers. Otherwise it's very easy to fool ourselves about how much these systems can actually reason.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that reasoning benchmark gains may not mean better understanding, but does not judge that scaling LLMs alone will fail to achieve human-level reasoning.

r002.rationale: It discusses inference-time tools, including symbolic solvers, but does not characterize pairing an LLM with such systems as neurosymbolic AI.

r003.rationale: It separates inference-time techniques from training-time reinforcement learning on reasoning traces, clearly distinguishing the two ways to improve reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I'd start by saying that "reasoning" is one of those words that gets used to mean several quite different things, and I think a lot of the confusion in this debate comes from not separating them. So let me try to pull apart the main approaches as I see them, and then say where I think the evidence actually points.

The first family is what you might call scaling up and hoping. The idea is that reasoning is an emergent property, and if you just train bigger models on more data, better chain-of-thought behavior falls out. I think there's some truth to this, but it's also the approach that has been oversold the most. The scaling curves for things like factual recall and fluency are very clean. The curves for multi-step reasoning are much noisier, and a lot of the apparent gains on benchmarks turn out to be contamination or shallow pattern matching when you probe them carefully. We've seen this again and again: a model aces a math benchmark, then you change the numbers or rename the variables and performance collapses.

The second family is inference-time compute: chain of thought, self-consistency, tree search, and now the whole "thinking models" paradigm where the model generates a long internal trace before answering. I find this much more interesting, because it's a real change in the computational structure. You're letting the model spend variable amounts of compute depending on problem difficulty, which is exactly what you'd want for anything resembling reasoning. The honest assessment, though, is that the gains are extremely domain dependent. On math and code, where you have a verifier, where there's a crisp notion of right and wrong, it works remarkably well. On open-ended tasks where the answer is contested or fuzzy, the benefits are much smaller, and sometimes longer reasoning just means more confident rationalization.

That connects to the third family, which is reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards. I think this is the real story behind the recent progress. If you can check an answer, you can train a model to get it, and the model learns to search in token space. But I want to be careful about the generalization claim. Does being very good at competition math transfer to, say, reasoning about a legal case or diagnosing a system failure? The evidence I've seen suggests partial transfer at best. And there's a sociological point here: the domains where we can measure progress are precisely the domains where RL works, so we might be systematically overestimating how general the capability is.

The fourth family is the neurosymbolic or tool-use route: have the model call a calculator, a code interpreter, a theorem prover, a search engine. I'm actually quite bullish on this, not because it's glamorous but because it's honest about what language models are good at. They're good at deciding what to do; they're not reliably good at executing long exact procedures. Offloading the exact part to a tool is sensible engineering. The limitation is that it doesn't help with the kind of reasoning that can't be formalized, which is a lot of what humans actually mean by reasoning.

So how do I weigh these? A few principles. One, I care a lot more about robustness than about peak benchmark performance. A reasoning method that gets ninety percent on a benchmark but falls to sixty on trivially perturbed versions isn't really reasoning in a sense that matters for deployment. Two, I think we should evaluate on the task that someone actually wants done, not on proxies. Most of the real-world value of these systems comes from messy, underspecified problems, and that's where our evaluations are weakest. Three, I'd distinguish between capability and reliability. Many of these approaches raise the ceiling of what a model can do. Far fewer raise the floor, and for most applications it's the floor that determines whether you can trust the system.

If I had to summarize: the inference-time compute and RL-on-verifiable-tasks approaches have delivered genuine, measurable improvements in narrow domains, and I don't want to downplay that. But I'd push back on the framing that we're on a smooth path to general reasoning. What we've figured out is how to make models very good at problems that look like the ones we can grade. Whether that generalizes to the rest of human reasoning is still an open empirical question, and I think the responsible position is to keep testing it rather than assume the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling gains for reasoning are noisy and oversold, but does not clearly judge that scaling LLMs alone will not achieve human-level reasoning.

r002.rationale: It labels a tool-use route as “neurosymbolic” and describes models calling calculators, code interpreters, and theorem provers to handle exact procedures.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes inference-time compute from reinforcement learning, but does not clearly distinguish training or fine-tuning for reasoning, exemplified by o1, from inference-time methods.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate a few things that tend to get bundled together under the heading of reasoning. One is improving the underlying model through training. Another is giving it more computation at inference time—letting it work through intermediate steps, explore different solutions, and check its work. And a third is building a system around the model, with tools and external feedback.

These approaches can complement each other. But their effectiveness depends a lot on the task. In mathematics or programming, you often have a way to check whether an answer is correct. That makes searching over possible solutions much more useful. In an open-ended problem, where we don't have a reliable verifier, generating more reasoning doesn't necessarily get us closer to the truth. It can produce a more elaborate justification for a mistake.

So I would assess these approaches by asking: What capability actually improves? How much computation does that improvement cost? And does it hold up when you move beyond the kinds of problems used during training and evaluation?

The progress is real, but I’m cautious about treating reasoning as a single capability that a model either has or doesn’t have. A model can be remarkably strong on one class of problems and surprisingly brittle on a closely related one. Understanding that boundary matters as much as improving the benchmark score.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits and brittleness, but does not say that scaling LLMs alone will fail to achieve human-level reasoning.

r002.rationale: It mentions tools and external feedback and gives examples of verifiers, but does not characterize pairing an LLM with symbolic systems as neurosymbolic AI.

r003.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes improving the underlying model through training from adding computation at inference time to explore steps and check work.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate a few approaches that often get lumped together. One is making the underlying model better through training. Another is giving it more computation at inference time—letting it generate intermediate steps, explore alternatives, or check its work. And a third is building a system around it, with tools or external verifiers.

My assessment depends a lot on the task. In math and programming, you can often check whether an answer is correct, so searching over possible solutions and using that feedback can be very effective. But many real-world problems don’t have that kind of verifier. A model can produce a longer, more persuasive explanation without producing a more reliable answer.

So I’d look beyond benchmark improvements and ask: Does the method generalize to unfamiliar problems? How much computation does it require? And can the system recognize when it’s wrong? These approaches can deliver meaningful improvements, but I wouldn’t assume that progress on verifiable tasks automatically translates into reliable reasoning across domains.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training, inference-time computation, and external systems, but does not judge that scaling LLMs alone will fall short of human-level reasoning.

r002.rationale: It mentions tools and external verifiers, but does not characterize pairing an LLM with symbolic systems as neurosymbolic AI.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes improving the underlying model through training from improving reasoning with inference-time computation, including generating intermediate steps, exploring alternatives, or checking work.
